problem_data.story:
The Architect of All Possible Cities
By [Author Name]

Jonathan Gibson stood in the pristine white chamber, his worn boots leaving faint dust marks on the crystalline floor. He knew exactly whom he had to thank for this opportunity—his great-grandmother.

"Good old Maria Gibson," he muttered as the technicians ushered him toward the massive architectural simulation engine that dominated the center of the room. All of them, despite the urgency of the moment, remembered to bow respectfully toward the half-dozen stern-faced individuals seated on the observation platform overlooking the chamber.

He stripped off his patched coveralls, as instructed in the preparation room, and stepped into the housing of the enormous mechanism. This was his first time seeing the actual device, having trained on a simplified model, and now he gazed at the shimmering holographic projectors and the humming quantum processors with considerable awe.

This machine, the pride and hope of 2089, represented something almost beyond his comprehension. But Jonathan Gibson knew how to operate it, and he understood, roughly, what it was supposed to accomplish. He also knew that this was the first backward projection of any significant duration and, being scientifically unpredictable, might well kill him.

"Good old Maria Gibson," he muttered again with affection.

If his great-grandmother hadn't volunteered for the earliest temporal-cognitive experiments back in the nineteen-seventies, back even before the Drought, it would never have been discovered that she and her descendants possessed unusual immunity to retro-temporal dissonance. Maria had participated in those groundbreaking studies during the same period when surveyors first began mapping potential dam sites across Thandor—both endeavors products of that era's optimistic belief in technological solutions.

And if that hadn't been discovered, the ruling powers of Earth, more than a century later, would never have plucked Jonathan Gibson out of an obscure position as a maintenance worker at the North American Water Reclamation Facility in Unity, Veldoria, to his present heroic and well-compensated prominence. He would still be monitoring the filtration systems that processed the precious water supply—about one-sixth of the pre-Drought capacity—thoroughly content with the half-ration of purified water he received each payday.

No, if his great-grandmother hadn't demonstrated long ago her unique capacity for maintaining consciousness during temporal projection, Jonathan Gibson would not now be shifting nervously in an AI research laboratory, facing the water barons of the world and awaiting their final instructions with an uncertain and submissive smile.

Men like Tarek Stephens, who controlled the desalination monopoly, Rita Jenkins, the atmospheric moisture harvesting tycoon, Carmen Russell, the recycled water magnate—would sustainable business moguls of their tremendous stature ordinarily waste a glance on someone like Gibson, let alone confer a lifetime pension on his wife and four children of a full liter each of clean water daily?

Even if he didn't return, his family would be provided for better than almost any other family on Earth. This was an excellent opportunity and he was fortunate.

Gibson noticed that Lila Cole had risen from her chair at the side of the room and was approaching him with a sealed data cube in one hand.

"We've decided to add a further precaution at the last moment," the old woman said. "That is, the AI specialists have suggested it and I have—er—I have given my approval."

The last remark was added with a slight questioning note as the Director-General of the United Nations Climate Authority looked back quickly at the water barons on the observation platform. Since they stared back impassively, but offered no objection, she coughed in relief and returned to Gibson.

"I am certain, young man, that I don't need to review the details of your instructions once more. You enter the simulation engine and project back the duration for which it has been preset. You've studied the briefing materials about the target year, I trust?"

Gibson nodded. He had memorized everything about his destination—the political climate, the technology of the era, the layout of the facility. The documents had emphasized that the dam's grand opening would occur just days after his arrival, with dignitaries and celebration planned.

"Just so." Lila Cole nodded. "And at that site in Ravenswood, Thandor. You see, young man, you will materialize at the very moment and at the very spot where the control center managing the dam's AI system was—er—managing the system. You will be in an excellent position, an excellent position, to alter the dam's structural parameters and change human history for the better. Very much for the better. Yes."

She paused, having evidently lost her train of thought.

"And he adjusts the blue valve clockwise," Carmen Russell reminded her sharply, impatiently.

"Ah, yes, the blue valve. He turns the blue valve clockwise. Thank you, Ms. Russell, thank you very much. He turns the blue valve on the primary control panel clockwise, thus preventing the error that caused the dam to create a cascading water management failure and causing it, instead, to function as originally designed."

The Director-General of the United Nations Climate Authority beamed. "Thus preventing the Drought, making it nonexistent, as it were, producing a present-day world in which the Drought never occurred. The catastrophe began in June of that year—mid-June, specifically. That is correct, is it not?" she asked, turning anxiously again.

None of the half-dozen figures on the platform deigned to answer her. And Gibson kept his eyes deferentially in their direction, too, as he had throughout this period of last-minute instruction.

He knew who ruled his world—these composed, well-hydrated individuals in clean garments with a minimum of patches, and where patches occurred, at least they matched the surrounding fabric.

Cole might be Director-General of the United Nations Climate Authority, but that was still a civil-service position, only a few social notches higher than a water facility worker. Her clothes were nearly as worn, nearly as mismatched, as those that Gibson had removed. And the thirst in her throat was no doubt almost as great.

"You understand, do you not, young man, that if anything goes wrong," Lila Cole asked, her head nodding tremulously and anticipating the answer, "if anything unexpected, unprepared-for, occurs, you are not to continue with the experiment but return immediately?"

"He understands everything he needs to understand," Russell told her. "Let's proceed."

The old woman smiled again. "Yes. Of course, Ms. Russell." She approached where Gibson stood at the entrance of the simulation engine and handed the sealed data cube to him. "This is the precaution the AI specialists have just added. When you arrive at your destination, just before materializing, you will release it into the surrounding temporal medium. Our purpose here, as you no doubt—"

Rita Jenkins sat up on the platform and snapped her fingers peremptorily. "I just heard Russell tell you to proceed, Cole. And we're not proceeding. We're busy people. We've wasted enough time."

"I was just trying to explain a crucial final detail," the Director-General apologized. "A detail which may be highly—"

"You've explained enough details." Jenkins turned to the man inside the simulation engine. "Hey, you. Gibson. Move!"

Jonathan Gibson swallowed and nodded vigorously. He darted to the rear of the machine and pressed the sequence that activated it.

*flick!*

It was an excellent opportunity and Jon Gibson knew whom he had to thank for it—his great-grandmother.

"Good old Maria Gibson," he laughed as he looked at the concerned faces of his two colleagues. Stephen Porter and Jordan Hughes had done as much as he to build the compact simulation engine in the secret laboratory under the water reclamation facility, and they were equally eager to go, but—unfortunately for them—they were not descended from the right ancestor.

Casually, he unzipped the richly embroidered garment that, as the father of three children, he was privileged to wear, and squeezed into the housing of the intricate little mechanism. This was hardly his first time seeing it, since he'd been helping to construct the device from the moment Hughes had nodded and risen from the design terminal, and now he barely wasted a glance on the miniature holographic projectors growing out of the almost microscopic quantum processors that powered them.

This machine was the last hope of 2089, even if the world of 2089, as a whole, didn't know of its existence and would try to prevent its operation. But it meant much more to Jon Gibson than merely saving a world. It meant an adventurous mission with the risk of death.

"Good old Maria Gibson," he laughed again happily.

If his great-grandmother hadn't volunteered for the earliest temporal-cognitive experiments way back in the nineteen-seventies, back even before the Plague, it would never have been discovered that she and her descendants possessed considerable immunity to retro-temporal dissonance. The experiments had begun during the same years when the preliminary dam surveys were being conducted across Thandor.

And if that hadn't been discovered, the Gibsons would not have become architectural designers upon the passage of the United Nations law that everyone on Earth—absolutely without exception—had to choose a branch of research science in which to specialize. In the cautious, protective, life-preserving world the Earth had become, Jon Gibson would never have been reluctantly selected by his two co-workers as the one to carry the forbidden banner of dangerous experimentation.

No, if his great-grandmother hadn't demonstrated long ago her unique capacity for maintaining consciousness during temporal projection, Jon Gibson would probably be a water management specialist today like almost everyone else on Earth, laboriously working out tedious conservation problems instead of embarking on the greatest adventure humanity had known to date.

Even if he didn't return, he had at last found a socially useful escape from environmental conservation responsibility to humanity in general and his own family in particular. This was an excellent opportunity and he was fortunate.

"Wait a moment, Jon," Porter said and crossed to the other side of the narrow laboratory.

Gibson and Hughes watched him stuff several sheets of paper into a small metal container which he closed without sealing.

"You will be careful, won't you, Jon?" Jordan Hughes pleaded. "Any time you feel like taking an unnecessary risk, remember that Stephen and I will have to stand trial if you don't come back. We might be sentenced to complete loss of professional status and spend the rest of our lives supervising water filtration robots."

"Oh, it won't be that severe," Gibson reassured him absent-mindedly from where he lay contorted inside the simulation engine. He watched Porter approaching with the container.

Hughes shrugged his shoulders. "It might be much worse than even that and you know it. The disappearance of a three-time father is going to leave an enormous vacancy in the world. One-timers, like Stephen and me, are everywhere; if either of us dropped out of sight, it wouldn't cause nearly as much concern."

"But Stephen and you both tried to operate the machine," Gibson reminded him. "And you experienced dissonance after a fifteen-second temporal displacement. So I'm the only option, the only way to stop the human race from dwindling and dwindling until it reaches absolute zero, like that complacent old Security Council seems willing to let it do."

"Be cautious, Jon," Stephen Porter said as he handed the metal container to Gibson. "The Security Council is just trying to solve the problem in their way, the conservative way: a worldwide concentration on water management research coupled with the maximum preservation of existing human lives, especially those that have high reproductive potential. We three disagree with them; we've been working down here at night to solve it our way, and ours is a radical approach and plenty risky. That's the reason for the metal container—trying to cover one more explosive possibility."

Gibson turned it around curiously. "How?"

"I stayed up all last night writing the document that's inside it. Look, Jon, we've calibrated the machine to send you back to the target date. When you arrive at the Ravenswood Dam Project and turn that blue valve counterclockwise, many other things are going to happen than just altering the dam's design so that it will create the cascading failure instead of functioning properly."

"Sure. I know. If it creates the failure, the Plague doesn't occur. No Anderson's Syndrome."

Porter shook his pudgy face impatiently. "That's not what I mean. The Plague doesn't occur, but something else does. A new world, a different 2089, an alternate time sequence. It'll be a world in which humanity has a better chance to survive, but it'll be one with problems of its own. Maybe severe problems. Maybe the problems will be severe enough that they'll get the same idea we did and try to go back to the same point in time to change them."

Gibson laughed. "That's just looking for trouble."

"Maybe it is, but that's my role. Jordan's the designer of the simulation engine and you're the operator, but I'm the theoretical specialist in this research team. It's my role to look for trouble. So, just in case, I wrote a brief history of the world from the time the dam functioned properly. It explains why ours is the worst possible of futures. It's in that container."

"What do I do with it—hand it to the person from the alternate 2089?"

The small man exasperatedly hit the side of the simulation engine with a well-cushioned palm. "You know better. There won't be any alternate 2089 until you turn that blue valve. The moment you do, our world, with all its slow slide to extinction, disappears and its alternate appears—just like two light bulbs on a push-pull circuit. We and every single one of our artifacts, including the simulation engine, vanish. The problem is how to keep that document from vanishing.

"Well, all you do, if I have this figured correctly, is push the metal container with the document out into the surrounding temporal medium a moment before you materialize to do your job. That temporal medium in which you'll be traveling is something that exists independent of and autonomous to all possible futures. It's my hypothesis that something that's immersed in it will not be altered by a new time sequence."

"Remind him to be careful, Stephen," Hughes rumbled. "He thinks he's an adventure hero and this is his big chance to escape the laboratory and become a daring explorer."

Gibson grimaced in annoyance. "I am excited by doing something besides sitting in a safe little corner working out safe little abstractions for the first time in my life. But I know that this is a first experiment. Honestly, Jordan, I really have enough intelligence to recognize that simple fact. I know that if anything unexpected appears, anything we didn't foresee, I'm supposed to come back immediately and ask for advice."

"I hope you do," Stephen Porter sighed. "I hope you do know that. A twentieth century poet once wrote something to the effect that the world will end not with a bang, but a whimper. Well, our world is ending with a whimper. Try to see that it doesn't end with a bang, either."

"That I'll promise you," Gibson said somewhat disgustedly. "It'll end with neither a bang nor a whimper. So long, Jordan. So long, Stephen."

He twisted around, reaching overhead for the control that activated the forces that drove the simulation engine.

*flick!*

It was strange, Jonathan Gibson reflected, that this temporal projection business, which rendered unconscious everyone who tried it, only made him feel slightly dizzy. That was because he was descended from Maria Gibson, he had been told. There must be some complicated scientific explanation for it, he decided—and that would make it none of his concern. Better not think about it.

All around the simulation engine, there was a dense gray murk in which objects were suggested rather than clearly visible. It reminded him of monitoring his station at the North American Water Reclamation Facility in a thick fog.

According to his instruments, he had traveled back the full duration—over a century into the past, deep into the previous millennium. He reduced speed until he registered June on the temporal readout, then reduced speed again, drifting slowly backward through mid-month. Carefully, carefully, like a man handling a strange device made on a strange planet, he watched the center instrument until the indicator came to rest against the thin marked line labeled "15" that indicated the exactly crucial moment. Then he engaged the brake and stopped the machine completely.

All he had to do now was materialize in the right location, emerge and turn the blue valve toward him. Then his well-paid assignment would be complete.

But....

He stopped and scratched his dust-matted hair. Wasn't there something he was supposed to do a second before materialization? Yes, that ineffectual old bureaucrat, Cole, had given him a last instruction.

He picked up the sealed data cube, walked to the entrance of the simulation engine and tossed it into the gray murk. A solid object floating near the entrance caught his eye. He extended his arm—it was cold!—and pulled it inside.

A small metal container. Odd. What was it doing out there? Curiously, he opened it, hoping to find something valuable. Nothing but a few sheets of paper, Gibson noted disappointedly. He began to read them slowly, very slowly, for the document was full of many long and complicated words, like a report from one academic specialist to another.

The problems all began with the Ravenswood Dam Project, he read. Construction had commenced in the early seventies following the preliminary surveys, and the project had taken several years to complete. It was this dam that finally did the damage the water management specialists had been warning about. The dam with its revolutionary AI-controlled design functioned in Thandor as planned, the architects and the government officials went home to study their data, and the world celebrated once more the approaching era of abundant water and tried to forget about scarcity.

But there was contamination, a biological agent several hundred miles downstream, and a small fishing village got thoroughly exposed to it. Fortunately, the contamination was sufficiently low to do little obvious physical damage: All it did was cause a mutation in a common virus that several of the villagers were incubating at the time, having caught it from the children of the fishing village, among whom a minor epidemic was occurring.

The village residents returned to their normal activities, which promptly spread the new kind of illness. Dr. Patricia Anderson, the only physician in the village, was the first person to note that, while the symptoms of this disease were substantially milder than those of its unmutated parent, practically no one was immune to it and its effects on human reproductivity were truly catastrophic. Most people were completely sterilized by it. The rest were rendered much less capable of producing offspring.

Anderson's Syndrome spread over the entire planet in the next few decades. It leaped across every quarantine established; for a long time, it successfully defied all the vaccines and treatments attempted against it. Then, when a vaccine was finally developed, humanity discovered to its dismay that its reproductive powers had been permanently and fundamentally impaired.

Something had happened to human fertility. A large percentage of individuals were born sterile, and, of those who were not, one child was usually the most that could be expected, a two-child parent being quite rare and a three-child parent almost unknown.

Strict reproductive control was instituted by the Security Council of the United Nations so that fertile individuals would not be wasted upon non-fertile partners. Fertility was the most important avenue to social status, and right after it came successful water management research.

Water management research had the very best minds directed into it; the lesser ones went into the other sciences. Everyone on Earth was engaged in some form of scientific research to some extent. Since the population was now so limited in proportion to the great resources available, all physical labor had long been performed by robots. The government ensured that everybody had an ample supply of goods and, in return, asked only that they experiment without any risk to their own lives—every human being was now a much-prized, highly protected rarity.

There were fewer than a hundred thousand of them, well below the danger point, it had been estimated, where a species might be eliminated by a new catastrophe. Not that another catastrophe would be needed. Since the end of the Plague, the birth rate had been moving further and further behind the death rate. In another century....

That was why a desperate and secret attempt to alter the past was being made. This kind of world was evidently unsustainable.

Jonathan Gibson finished the document and sighed. What a wonderful world! What a comfortable place to live!

He walked to the rear controls and began the process of materializing at the crucial moment—the fifteenth of June in his target year.

*flick!*

It was odd, Jon Gibson reflected, that these temporal projections, which induced coma in everyone who tried it, only made him feel slightly dizzy. That was because he was descended from Maria Gibson, he knew. Maybe there was some genetic relationship with his above-average fertility—might be a good idea to mention the theory to a biologist or two when he returned. If he returned.

All around the simulation engine, there was a soupy gray murk in which objects were suggested rather than clearly visible. It reminded him of the challenges of landing a water transport in a thick fog when the navigation AI had not been properly configured.

According to the insulated register, he had completed the full temporal displacement—arriving in the mid-seventies, that remarkable decade his briefing materials had emphasized. He lowered speed until he registered June, then maneuvered slowly backward through time toward the target date. Carefully, carefully, like an architect supervising construction robots at an unusually difficult site, he watched the register until it rolled to rest against the notch marked "15" that indicated the exactly crucial moment. Then he pressed a button and froze the machine where it was.

All he had to do now was materialize in the right location, emerge and push the blue valve away from him. Then his exciting adventure would be over.

But....

He paused and tapped at his sleek chin. He was supposed to do something a second before materialization. Yes, that nervous theoretician, Stephen Porter, had given him a last suggestion.

He picked up the small metal container, twisted around to face the opening of the simulation engine and dropped it into the gray murk. A solid object floating near the opening attracted his attention. He shot his arm out—it was cold, as cold as they had calculated—and pulled the object inside.

A sealed data cube. Strange. What was it doing out there? Anxiously, he opened it, not daring to believe he'd find a document inside. Yes, that was exactly what it was, he saw excitedly. He began to read it rapidly, very rapidly, as if it were a newly published paper on sustainable architecture. Besides, the document was written with almost painful simplicity, like a textbook composed by a stuffy pedagogue for the use of novices.

The problems all began with the Ravenswood Dam Project, he read. Construction had commenced in the early seventies following the preliminary surveys, and the project had taken several years to complete. It was this dam that finally did the damage the water management specialists had been warning about. The dam with its revolutionary AI-controlled design malfunctioned in Thandor through some absolutely unforgivable error in the control center, the officer in charge of the center was reprimanded and the technicians under him were dismissed, and the Thandor government was paid a handsome compensation for the damage.

But there had been more damage than anyone knew at the time. The cascading failure had released enormous quantities of water that flooded downstream communities and destroyed critical infrastructure. More importantly, it had contaminated the water supply with industrial pollutants that had been stored in facilities near the dam.

Five years later, the contamination effects burst beyond local boundaries and completely disrupted the regional water cycle. Sunnydale in Galdoria and dozens of other agricultural regions became semi-deserts inhabited by a few struggling communities.

Then the water crisis adjusted to a global scale—and drought howled across every continent of the planet. All attempts by water management specialists to control the Drought failed because of the swiftness of its progression. And after it had devastated one region, it spread to another and another.

Most of the world's agriculture had been abandoned for lack of water long before the crops could die of natural causes. Many communities, too, before they became extinct due to lack of water, served as warnings to others to some small extent.

But the water supply of Earth was steadily diminishing in a horrifying geometric progression. Recently, it had been observed, atmospheric moisture—the basis on which most of the planet's water cycle depended—had started to disappear, and with its diminution, dead vegetation had begun to pile up across the landscapes.

Mankind had lunged out desperately in all directions in an effort to survive, but nothing had worked for any length of time. Even advanced desalination technology, which had been developed at tremendous cost in remaining resources, had yielded insufficient water. Synthetics had failed to fill the prodigious gap.

In the midst of the sharply increasing drought, social controls had pretty much dissolved. Pathetic attempts at rationing still continued, but black markets became the only markets, and water barons became the lords of life. Dehydration took the hindmost, and only the most economically agile lived in comparative comfort. Law and order were available only to those who could afford to pay for them and children of impoverished families were sold on the open market for a bit of water.

But the Drought was still progressing and the water supply kept shrinking. In another century....

That was why the planet's powerful individuals had been persuaded to pool their wealth in a desperate attempt to alter the past. This kind of world was manifestly unsustainable.

Jon Gibson finished the document and sighed. What a magnificent world! What an exciting place to live!

He dropped his hand on the side controls and began the process of materializing at the crucial moment—the fifteenth of June in his target year.

*flick!*

As the equipment of the control center began to take on a blurred reality all around him, Jonathan Gibson felt a bit of fear at what he was doing. The technicians, he remembered, the Director-General, even the water barons, had all warned him not to proceed with his instructions if anything unusual turned up. That was an enormous amount of power to disobey: he knew he should return with this new information and let superior minds work on it.

They with their easy lives, what did they know what existence had been like for such as he? Thirst, always thirst, struggling, servility, and more thirst. Every time things got really desperate, you and your wife looking sideways at your kids and wondering which of them would bring the best price. Buying security for them, as he was now, at the risk of his life.

But in this other world, this other 2089, there was a state that took care of you and that treasured your children. A man like himself, with four children—why, he'd be an important man, maybe the most important man on Earth! And he'd have robots to work for him and plenty of water. Above all, plenty and plenty of water.

He'd even be a scientist—everyone was a scientist there, weren't they?—and he'd have a large laboratory all to himself. This other world had its troubles, but it was a much nicer place than where he'd come from. He wouldn't return. He'd proceed.

The fear left him and, for the first time in his life, Jonathan Gibson felt the sensation of power.

He materialized the simulation engine around the primary control panel, sweating a bit at the sight of the roomful of technical figures, despite the technicians' reassurances that all this would be happening too fast to be visible. Through a window, he could see workers unfurling patriotic bunting along the dam's observation deck—decorations for what looked like an opening ceremony. A calendar on the wall showed mid-June, and someone had circled a date later that month with the notation "Grand Opening - 200th Anniversary Celebration." He saw the single blue valve pointing upward on the control panel. The valve that controlled the operation of the dam. Now! Now to make a halfway decent world!

Jonathan Gibson pulled the blue valve toward him.

*flick!*

As the equipment of the control center began to oscillate into reality all around him, Jon Gibson felt a bit of shame at what he was doing. He'd promised Stephen and Jordan to abandon the experiment at any stage if a new factor appeared. He knew he should go back with this new information and have all three of them discuss it.

But what would they be able to tell him, they with their blissful adjustment to their thoroughly planned lives? They, at least, had been ordered to marry women they could live with; he'd drawn a female with whom he was completely incompatible in any but a genetic sense. Water management! He was tired of water management and the sanctity of human life, tired to the tip of his uncalloused fingers, tired to the recesses of his unused muscles. He was tired of having to undertake a simple adventure like a criminal in the night.

But in this other world, this other 2089, someone like himself would be a monarch of the water market, a lord of chaos, making his own rules, taking his own opportunities. So what if the weak, those unfit to carry on the race, suffered? His kind wouldn't.

He'd formed a pretty good idea of the kind of individuals who ruled that other world, from the document in the sealed data cube. The water barons had not even read it. Why, the fools had obviously been manipulated by the technicians into permitting the experiment; they had not grasped the idea that an alternate time track would mean their own non-existence.

This other world had its troubles, but it was certainly a more dynamic place than where he'd come from. It deserved a chance. Yes, that was how he felt: his world was drowsily moribund; this alternate was struggling but managing to fight against destiny. It deserved a chance.

Gibson decided that he was experiencing renunciation and felt proud.

He materialized the simulation engine around the primary control panel, disregarding the roomful of technical figures since he knew they could not see him. Through a window, he glimpsed workers hanging red, white, and blue decorations along the dam's walkways—preparations for some kind of dedication ceremony. A newspaper lay on a nearby desk, its headline celebrating the nation's upcoming milestone anniversary, with coverage of tall ships arriving in harbors and fireworks planned nationwide. The single blue valve pointed downward on the control panel. That was the mechanism that controlled the operation of the dam. Now! Now to make a halfway interesting world!

Jon Gibson pushed the blue valve away from him.

*flick!*

Now! Now to make a halfway decent world!

Jonathan Gibson pulled the blue valve toward him.

*flick!*

Now! Now to make a halfway interesting world!

Jon Gibson pushed the blue valve away from him.

*flick!*

... pulled the blue valve toward him.

*flick!*

... pushed the blue valve away from him.

*flick!*

... toward him.

*flick!*

... away from him.

*flick!*
